Quick revision sheet

Number System, LCM & HCF

CUET GAT · General Test 501
6number families
2big ideas: HCF and LCM
6divisibility tests
30–45 starget per question
One-line methodClassify the number → choose the rule → prime-factorise → lowest powers for HCF, highest for LCM → verify with HCF × LCM.
The method
  1. Classify the numbers: Classify the numbers in the question: prime, composite, even, odd, fraction.
  2. Pick the rule: Pick the matching rule: divisibility test, HCF or LCM, remainder, or factor count.
  3. Prime factorise: Break the numbers into prime factors when two or more numbers are involved.
  4. Apply HCF or LCM: Apply the rule: HCF takes the lowest powers, LCM takes the highest powers.
  5. Verify the result: Check with HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers, or by substituting.
Formulas and facts
Number families
FamilyMeaningExamples
Natural numbersCounting numbers starting from 11, 2, 3, 4 ...
Whole numbersNatural numbers together with 00, 1, 2, 3 ...
IntegersWhole numbers and their negatives−3, 0, 5
Prime numbersExactly two factors: 1 and itself (2 is the only even prime)2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13
Composite numbersMore than two factors (1 is neither prime nor composite)4, 6, 9, 12
Rational numbersCan be written as p/q with q not zero3/4, −2, 0.5
Divisibility tests
Divisible byRuleExample
3Digit sum divisible by 34,572: 4+5+7+2 = 18 ✓
4Last two digits divisible by 47,316: 16 ✓
6Divisible by both 2 and 31,254: even, digit sum 12 ✓
8Last three digits divisible by 85,128: 128 = 8 × 16 ✓
9Digit sum divisible by 96,381: 6+3+8+1 = 18 ✓
11(Sum of odd-place digits) − (sum of even-place digits) is 0 or a multiple of 112,728: (2+2) − (7+8) = −11 ✓
HCF and LCM
IdeaMethodExample
Prime factorisationWrite each number as a product of primes12 = 2²×3, 18 = 2×3²
HCFCommon primes at the LOWEST power2 × 3 = 6
LCMAll primes at the HIGHEST power2² × 3² = 36
RelationHCF × LCM = product of the two numbers6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18
Number of factorsN = p^a × q^b gives (a+1)(b+1) factors72 = 2³×3² gives 4 × 3 = 12
Division factDividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder100 = 7 × 14 + 2
Core ideas in a line
  • Why prime factorisation is the master key. Every whole number above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way.
  • How divisibility tests really work. Our number system is built on powers of 10.
  • HCF versus LCM in everyday words. HCF answers 'the biggest piece that fits exactly into every length', such as the largest tile or the greatest number of equal groups.
Question styles
StyleExampleMethod
Divisibility checkWhich of the following numbers is divisible by 9Apply the digit-sum test to every option.
HCF / LCM word problemLargest tile that fits a floor; bells ringing together'Largest' points to HCF, 'smallest' points to LCM.
Remainder problemNumber leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, 6 and 8Use LCM plus the common remainder.
Factors and primesNumber of factors of 60; primes between 10 and 30Use (a+1)(b+1) or list the primes.
Missing digitFind the digit x so that 5x72 is divisible by 9Digit-sum test with an unknown.
PropertiesSmallest prime; sum of two odd numbersDirect recall of number facts.
Tricks and why they work
#TrickHowWhy it works
1Use the digit sum for 3 and 9Add the digits. If the sum is divisible by 3 the number is; if it is divisible by 9 the number is divisible by 9.Every place value (10, 100, 1000 ...) leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9, so a number behaves like its digit sum.
2'Largest' means HCF, 'smallest' means LCMLargest number that divides all: HCF. Smallest number divisible by all: LCM.HCF is never larger than the smallest number given; LCM is never smaller than the largest. 'Divides' and 'divisible by' point in opposite directions.
3Remainder trick: LCM plus the common remainderIf N leaves remainder r with divisors a, b, c, then N = LCM(a,b,c) × k + r.N − r is divisible by every divisor, so N − r is a multiple of the LCM.
4When the gap is common, subtract itIf each remainder is 1 less than its divisor, N = LCM × k − 1.Then N + 1 is divisible by every divisor, so N + 1 is a multiple of the LCM.
5Count factors from the primesWrite N as p^a × q^b × r^c. Factors = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1).Each factor picks a power of p from 0 to a, of q from 0 to b, and so on; the choices multiply.
6Verify with HCF × LCMFor two numbers, HCF × LCM must equal their product.Each prime appears once at its lowest power (in HCF) and once at its highest (in LCM), so together they give both exponents.
7Co-prime numbers have HCF 1If two numbers share no prime factor, their LCM is simply their product.With no common prime, the product already contains every prime of each number exactly once.
8Largest divisor that leaves given remaindersTo find the largest number dividing a, b and c leaving remainders r₁, r₂, r₃, take the HCF of (a − r₁), (b − r₂), (c − r₃).Subtracting the remainders makes each number exactly divisible by the required divisor.
9Test a prime only up to its square rootTo test 91, test primes up to 9: 7 divides it (7 × 13).If a number has a factor larger than its square root, it must also have one smaller than its square root.
Speed hacks
  • 3 and 9: add the digits. 11: alternate-digit difference. 4 and 8: check the last 2 and 3 digits.
  • HCF goes down, LCM goes up: lowest powers for HCF, highest powers for LCM.
  • Two numbers only: HCF × LCM = a × b. Co-prime numbers have HCF 1 and LCM = product.
  • Factor count: add 1 to each exponent and multiply (72 = 2³·3² gives 4 × 3 = 12).
  • Prime check: test only the primes up to the square root (for 97, test 2, 3, 5, 7).
  • Remainders: N = LCM × k + r. If every remainder is 1 short of its divisor, N = LCM × k − 1.
Worked examples
ExampleQuestionAnswer
Example 1 · DivisibilityTest whether 4,572 is divisible by 9 using the digit sum4,572 is divisible by 9 (and therefore also by 3).
Example 2 · HCF and LCMFind the HCF and LCM of 24 and 36HCF = 12, LCM = 72.
Example 3 · Largest tileA room 8 m 40 cm long and 6 m 30 cm wide is tiled with square tiles. Find the largest tileThe largest tile has a side of 210 cm.
Example 4 · RemainderFind the smallest number that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, 6 and 8N = 27.
Example 5 · Common-gap trapFind the smallest number which leaves remainder 4 when divided by 5 and remainder 6 when divided by 7N = 34. Check: 34 = 5×6 + 4 = 7×4 + 6.
Example 6 · Largest divisor with remaindersFind the largest number that divides 60 and 75 leaving remainders 4 and 5The largest such number is 14. Check: 60 = 14 × 4 + 4 and 75 = 14 × 5 + 5.

Quick revision sheet

Simplification, Approximation & Surds

CUET GAT · General Test 501
6steps in BODMAS
6surd and power rules
2approximation moves
30 starget per question
One-line methodBrackets, then 'of', then ÷ and × left to right, then + and − left to right; for approximation round first.
The method
  1. Scan the expression: Scan the expression for brackets, 'of', powers and roots.
  2. Brackets first: Resolve the brackets from the innermost outward.
  3. Powers, of, × and ÷: Do powers and roots, then 'of', then division and multiplication from left to right.
  4. Then + and −: Finish with addition and subtraction from left to right.
  5. Round for approximation: For approximation, round every number first, then calculate.
Formulas and facts
BODMAS order
LetterStands forNote
BBrackets ( ) { } [ ]Innermost bracket first
OOfMeans multiply; done before division and multiplication
DDivisionSame rank as M; work left to right
MMultiplicationSame rank as D; work left to right
AAdditionSame rank as S; work left to right
SSubtractionDone last, left to right
Surd and power rules
RuleMeaningExample
√a × √b = √(ab)Multiply under one root√2 × √8 = √16 = 4
√a ÷ √b = √(a/b)Divide under one root√18 ÷ √2 = √9 = 3
(√a)² = aSquaring cancels the root(√7)² = 7
(a+b)(a−b) = a² − b²Difference of squares103 × 97 = 100² − 3² = 9,991
1/(√a + √b) = (√a − √b)/(a − b)Rationalising the denominator1/(√3+1) = (√3−1)/2
x% of y = y% of xSwap to the easier one8% of 50 = 50% of 8 = 4
Values worth knowing by heart
GroupValuesUse
Squares 11 to 15121, 144, 169, 196, 225Quick square-root and a²−b² work
Cubes 1 to 61, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216Cube-root and series questions
Surd values√2 ≈ 1.414, √3 ≈ 1.732, √5 ≈ 2.236Estimating answers with roots
Core ideas in a line
  • Why the order of operations exists. Mathematics needs one agreed order so that an expression has exactly one value.
  • Left to right inside the same rank. Division and multiplication share a rank, as do addition and subtraction, so inside a rank you simply work from left to right.
  • When rounding is safe in approximation. Approximation questions give options that are spread apart, so each number can be rounded to the nearest convenient value.
Question styles
StyleExampleMethod
Pure BODMASSimplify 18 + 2 × (5 + 3) − ¼ of 40Straight application of the order.
Fractions and decimalsSimplify 0.6 × 0.5 + 3/4 of 2Convert to one form first.
SurdsSimplify √12 × √3, or rationalise 1/(√5 − 2)Use the surd rules.
ApproximationFind the approximate value of 39.8% of 601Round to 40% of 600.
Missing valueFind x if 45 + 12 × x ÷ 4 = 63Undo the operations in reverse order.
Squares and identitiesValue of (2.5)² − (1.5)²Use a² − b² = (a+b)(a−b).
Tricks and why they work
#TrickHowWhy it works
1Work from the innermost bracket outwardRewrite the expression after each step. Never do two operations at once.Skipping lines is how order and sign errors enter, and a wrong value earns no marks however fast it was found.
2'Of' is multiplication that goes firstIn '¼ of 40 + 6', do ¼ of 40 = 10 first, then add 6.'Of' ties a fraction to its object like a bracket, so it is resolved before the result is divided or multiplied further.
3Use a² − b² for near-pairs103 × 97 = 100² − 3². 52 × 48 = 50² − 2².Numbers equally far from a round number multiply to the square of the centre minus the square of the gap.
4Round to friendly numbers, then calculate49.8 × 19.9 ≈ 50 × 20 = 1,000.Rounding shifts each number by under 1%, while options in approximation questions usually differ by 5% or more.
5Rationalise with the conjugateMultiply top and bottom by the same expression with the middle sign flipped.(√a + √b)(√a − √b) = a − b, which removes the root from the denominator.
6Reverse BODMAS for a missing valueUndo the last operation first: undo + and −, then ÷ and ×.Solving is BODMAS run backwards, so the last step performed is the first undone.
7Pair up numbers that make round valuesIn 25 × 17 × 4 do 25 × 4 = 100 first, then 100 × 17 = 1,700.Multiplication does not depend on order, so grouping friendly pairs removes work.
8Squares of numbers ending in 5For 35², compute 3 × 4 = 12 and append 25 to get 1,225.(10a + 5)² = 100a(a + 1) + 25.
9Add surds only when they are alike√12 + √3 = 2√3 + √3 = 3√3.Only surds with the same root part can be added, so simplify each one first.
Speed hacks
  • BODMAS: Brackets, Of, Division, Multiplication, Addition, Subtraction. D and M are equals, A and S are equals: go left to right.
  • Near pairs: 103 × 97 = 100² − 3² (a² − b²).
  • Squares ending in 5: n5² = n(n + 1) followed by 25 (35² = 1,225).
  • Approximation: round to friendly numbers (25, 50, 100); the options are far apart.
  • Rationalise with the conjugate: 1/(√a + √b) = (√a − √b)/(a − b).
  • x% of y = y% of x: pick whichever is easier.
Worked examples
ExampleQuestionAnswer
Example 1 · Basic BODMASSimplify 18 + 2 × (5 + 3) − ¼ of 4018 + 16 − 10 = 24.
Example 2 · FractionsSimplify 3/4 of 48 ÷ 6 + 56 + 5 = 11.
Example 3 · SurdsSimplify √12 × √3 + (√5)²6 + 5 = 11.
Example 4 · RationaliseRationalise 1/(√5 − 2)1/(√5 − 2) = √5 + 2.
Example 5 · ApproximationFind the approximate value of 39.8% of 601The value is about 240 (exact value 239.198).
Example 6 · Powers and rootsSimplify (7² − 5²) ÷ √36 + 3 × 44 + 12 = 16.

Quick revision sheet

Percentage & Its Applications

CUET GAT · General Test 501
%means per 100
6core formulas
8fraction pairs to know
30–45 starget per question
One-line methodFind the base → convert to a multiplier → apply each change on the latest value → compare with the base.
The method
  1. Find the base: Identify the base, the quantity that counts as 100%: original price, total, or old value.
  2. Convert to multipliers: Convert each percentage into a fraction or multiplier (20% = 1/5, +20% = ×1.2).
  3. Apply changes in order: Apply the changes one after another, each on the latest value.
  4. Compare with the base: Compare the final value with the base to get the net change.
  5. Sanity-check the direction: Check the direction of the answer (increase or decrease) against common sense.
Formulas and facts
Fraction and percentage pairs
FractionPercentageMultiplier for the increase
1/250%×1.5
1/3≈ 33.3%×1.333
1/425%×1.25
1/520%×1.2
1/6≈ 16.7%×1.167
1/812.5%×1.125
1/1010%×1.1
1/12≈ 8.33%×1.083
Core formulas
IdeaFormulaExample
Percentage(Part ÷ Whole) × 10018 out of 60 = 30%
Increase or decreaseNew = Old × (1 ± r/100)₹800 raised 15% = ₹920
Percentage change(Change ÷ Original) × 10040 to 50 = 25% increase
Successive changes a% and b%Net = a + b + ab/100+20% then +10% = +32%
A is x% more than BB is x/(100 + x) × 100 % less than A25% more means 20% less
Percentage pointsCompare the percentages directly20% to 25% = +5 points, +25% growth
Core ideas in a line
  • Percent is a fraction in disguise. Every percentage is a fraction with denominator 100, so 35% is 35/100 = 7/20.
  • Why successive changes multiply. If a value rises 10% it becomes 1.1 times itself; a further rise of 20% multiplies that new value by 1.2.
  • Percentage versus percentage points. A change from 40% to 50% is 10 percentage points, but it is a 25% rise in the percentage itself (10 ÷ 40).
Question styles
StyleExampleMethod
Direct percentageFind 35% of 240Convert to a fraction or use 10% steps.
Percentage changeA price rises from ₹80 to ₹100Change divided by the OLD value.
Successive changeIncrease by 20% and then decrease by 20%Multiply the multipliers.
ComparisonA's salary is 25% more than B's; B's is how much lessUse the x/(100+x) rule.
Growth over yearsA population of 20,000 grows 10% a year for 2 yearsRepeat the multiplier.
Votes and marksA candidate gets 45% of the votes and loses by 300Use the difference of the percentages.
Tricks and why they work
#TrickHowWhy it works
1Find the base firstAsk 'percent of what' and treat that quantity as 100%.Every percentage question hides a base. The right method on the wrong base gives the wrong answer.
2Use multipliers, not steps+20% is ×1.2 and −20% is ×0.8, so +20% then −20% is ×0.96, a 4% fall.A multiplier folds the whole change into one multiplication, so long chains become one line.
3Learn the fraction pairs12.5% = 1/8, so 12.5% of 240 = 240 ÷ 8 = 30.A percentage becomes a division by a small whole number, which is quicker than decimal multiplication.
4Reverse percentage: divide, do not subtractIf a price after a 20% rise is 960, the original is 960 ÷ 1.2 = 800.The 20% was taken on the original, so the final value is 120% of the original; undo it by dividing by 1.2.
5x% of y = y% of x35% of 40 = 40% of 35 = 14.Both equal x × y / 100, so choose whichever is easier.
6Percentage points are not percent20% to 25% is 5 percentage points but 25% growth.Points compare the two percentages directly; percent change compares them relative to the starting value.
7Use 10% as the building blockFor 35% of 240 find 10% = 24, then 3.5 × 24 = 84.10% is a single decimal shift, and other percentages are multiples of it.
8Compare using percentagesTo compare 3/8 with 0.37, convert: 3/8 = 37.5%, which is larger than 37%.Converting both numbers to percentages puts them on a common scale.

Tricks and why they work
#TrickHowWhy it works
1Convert ratios to partsA ratio of 2 : 3 means 5 equal parts, 2 for the first and 3 for the second.A ratio only says how many equal parts each quantity has, so the total is the sum of the parts.
2Find the value of one part firstIf the numbers are in the ratio 3 : 5 and differ by 20, then 2 parts = 20 and 1 part = 10.Once one part is known every term is a simple multiple of it.
3Work with sums for averagesSum = average × count. Compare the old sum with the new sum.An average is a sum in disguise, and sums can be added and subtracted directly.

8Ages in a ratio after some yearsAges in the ratio 3 : 4 now: the age difference (1 part) never changes, so use it as the fixed anchor.Both people age equally, so their difference stays constant.

One-line methodList and sort → mean = sum ÷ n → middle value for the median → most frequent for the mode.
The method
  1. List the data: List the data and count the number of values, n.
  2. Sort ascending: Sort the data in ascending order (needed for the median and the mode).
  3. Find the mean: Compute the mean = sum ÷ n.
  4. Find the median: Find the median: the middle value (odd n) or the average of the two middle values (even n).
  5. Find the mode: Find the mode: the value with the highest frequency.
Formulas and facts

Core ideas in a line
  • Three measures, three ideas of the centre. The mean uses every value, so it balances the data but is pulled by extremes.
  • What changes when the data changes. Adding the same number to every value shifts the mean, median and mode by that number.
  • Spread and grouped data. The range (largest minus smallest) is the simplest measure of spread.

Tricks and why they work
#TrickHowWhy it works
1Sort first, alwaysWrite the data in order before finding the median or the mode.The median is defined by position in the ordered list, so unsorted data gives a wrong middle.
2The median position is (n + 1)/2For 7 values it is the 4th value; for 8 values, the average of the 4th and 5th.The middle sits halfway through the list; with an even count there are two middle values.
3Work with sums for the meanSum = mean × count; new mean = new sum ÷ new count.A mean is a sum divided by a count, so changing the data changes the sum and the count.
4Shift and scaleAdding k to every value adds k to the mean; multiplying by k multiplies the mean by k.Every value moves by the same rule, so their average moves by the same rule.
5The median resists outliersOne huge value pulls the mean but hardly moves the median.The median depends only on position, whereas the mean uses the size of every value.

The method

Core ideas in a line

  • Letters as numbers. Alphabet series are number series in disguise.

Tricks and why they work

1Take differences firstSubtract each term from the next and look at the gaps.Most number series are built by adding something, so the gaps expose the rule.
2Take differences of differencesIf the gaps are 4, 6, 8, 10, their gaps are 2, 2, 2.A constant second difference means a quadratic pattern such as n(n + 1).

Tricks and why they work
#TrickHowWhy it works
1Draw, never imagineUse + (or a square) for male, − (or a circle) for female, = between a married couple, a vertical line downward for children and a horizontal line for brothers and sisters. Put the older generation higher up.A tree turns a sentence into a picture, and the eye can see a relation that the mind has to calculate. Every top scorer in this chapter draws, even for two-line questions.
2Always start from the END of the chain and shorten step by stepFor 'A's father's brother's son', solve left to right in pairs: father's brother = uncle; uncle's son = cousin. The answer is 'A's cousin'. Never try to jump to the answer in one go.Each pair collapses into one relation word, so a long chain shrinks by one word every step and you can check each step against the table.
3Use the 'only' word as a key'My father's only son' is me (if I am male) or my brother (if I am female). 'My mother's only daughter' is me (if I am female) or my sister (if I am male). Without 'only' you cannot say it is the same person.'Only' means there is exactly one such child, so if the speaker fits, the speaker is that child. The question setter uses this to hide the speaker inside the chain.
4Identify the speaker first in pointing questionsIn 'Pointing to a girl, Neha said "She is the daughter of my father's only son"', start with Neha: she is female, so her father's only son is her brother. The girl is her brother's daughter, which is Neha's niece.Everything after the word 'my' is measured from the speaker. If you start from the pointed person you will reverse the answer, which is the most common mistake.
5The two-step rule for in-lawsAn in-law is always my spouse's relative or my relative's spouse. 'Wife's brother' and 'sister's husband' are both brothers-in-law; 'brother's wife' and 'husband's sister' are both sisters-in-law.Marriage joins two families. People who enter your family by marriage, or whose family you enter by marriage, are in-laws; blood relatives of those two families are not your blood relatives.
6Generation arithmeticWrite +1 for each step up (parent) and −1 for each step down (child). The final number tells the level of the answer: +1 is an uncle, aunt or parent; 0 is a sibling or cousin; −1 is a child, nephew or niece.You can instantly reject any option on the wrong level without finishing the chain. This saves 15 to 20 seconds.
7Side-pairing for uncles, aunts and cousinsFather's side: chacha / tau (uncle), bua (aunt). Mother's side: mama (uncle), mausi (aunt). 8Coded relations: translate, then drawWrite each symbol's meaning above it, solve the first pair, then bring in the next symbol. Never solve the whole code in one go.A code is only a short direct chain in disguise. Replacing symbols with words puts you back on familiar ground.

One-line methodStandard form → Venn diagram → keep what holds in every diagram → test each conclusion.
The method
  1. Standard form: Write each statement in standard form: All, No, Some, or Some-not.
  2. Draw Venn diagrams: Draw a Venn diagram for each statement (more than one diagram if the statement allows).
  3. Keep what always holds: Combine the diagrams and keep only the relations that hold in EVERY possible diagram.
  4. Test the conclusions: Test each conclusion: it follows only if it is true in all the diagrams.
  5. Either–Or check: If two conclusions are complementary and neither follows alone, check for 'Either–Or'.

Core ideas in a line
  • Logic, not real life. A syllogism is judged by its form, not by the world.
  • The role of the middle term. In 'All A are B' and 'All B are C', the term B appears in both statements but not in the conclusion; it links them.
  • Definite and possible conclusions. A conclusion follows only if it is true in every diagram.

Tricks and why they work
#TrickHowWhy it works
1Draw a Venn diagram for every statementAll = inside, No = separate circles, Some = overlap.A picture shows what must be true and what is only possible.
2'All A are B' does not mean 'All B are A''All cats are animals' does not mean 'All animals are cats'.A can sit inside B with room to spare, so B has members outside A.
3Only 'Some' and 'No' convert exactlySome A are B gives Some B are A. No A is B gives No B is A.Overlap and separation are symmetric relations.
4A conclusion follows only if it holds in ALL diagramsIf it is true in one diagram but false in another, it does not follow.The statements allow every diagram that fits them, so 'follows' means true in each.
5Ignore real-world knowledge'Some doctors are lions' may be false in life but valid if the statements say so.The exam tests logic, not facts.
6Either–Or: complementary pairs'Some A are B' and 'No A is B' together cover every case.One of them must be true, so if neither follows alone, 'either or' follows.
7Some plus All gives SomeSome A are B and All B are C give Some A are C.The overlap sits inside B, which sits inside C.
8No plus All gives Some-notNo A is B and All B are C give Some C are not A.The B members inside C are not A.
9Two negatives give nothingNo A is B and No B is C: there is no definite conclusion.Both being separate says nothing about A and C.

  • A conclusion follows only if it is true in EVERY diagram.
  • Ignore real-world facts; use only the statements.
  • Two negatives give no conclusion.
  • Either–Or: 'Some' and 'No' together cover every case.
